stem: A 26-year-old woman has a metastatic tumor in the lung. Biopsy shows large anaplastic cells with pleomorphic nuclei, and light microscopy cannot identify the tissue of origin. Immunohistochemistry shows strong staining for cytokeratin, with no staining for vimentin, desmin, GFAP or neurofilament.
oneliner: 26F + metastatic anaplastic tumor of unknown origin + strong cytokeratin staining, negative for vimentin, desmin, GFAP, neurofilament → which tissue of origin?
ask: Which tissue of origin does this stain pattern indicate?

whyNot.A: **Mesenchymal** tumors stain for vimentin, which is negative here
whyNot.B: **Skeletal muscle** tumors stain for desmin, which is negative here
whyNot.C: **Glial** tumors stain for GFAP, which is negative here
whyNot.E: **Neuronal** tumors stain for neurofilament, which is negative here

why: Intermediate filaments are **tissue-specific**, so they identify an anaplastic tumor's origin. **Cytokeratin** is expressed by **epithelial cells**; a cytokeratin-positive tumor with no other filament is a **carcinoma**.

idea.rule: Cytokeratin = epithelium, vimentin = mesenchyme, desmin = muscle, GFAP = glia, neurofilament = neurons.
also: Vimentin: connective tissue, fibroblasts, endothelium
Desmin: muscle (rhabdomyosarcoma)
GFAP: astrocytes (glioblastoma)
Neurofilament: neurons

stem: A 76-year-old man with advanced dementia lives alone and has lost 11 kg over several months. His BMI is 14. He has temporal and hand muscle wasting, sparse brittle hair and swollen legs. Liver tests are normal and urinalysis shows no protein.
oneliner: 76M + dementia + 11-kg weight loss + BMI 14 + temporal wasting + leg edema + normal liver tests, no proteinuria → which labs?
ask: Which set of laboratory results is most likely?

options.B: Low albumin, prealbumin, transferrin and lymphocytes
options.D: Normal albumin and prealbumin, high lymphocytes
options.E: Low albumin with high bilirubin and INR

whyNot.A: That is **nephrotic syndrome**; his urine has no protein
whyNot.C: That is **Cushing syndrome**, which brings central obesity, not a **BMI of 14** with wasting
whyNot.D: Normal values would not explain edema; severe malnutrition **lowers** these
whyNot.E: That is **liver failure**; his liver tests are normal

answer: Low albumin, prealbumin, transferrin and lymphocyte count
why: Severe protein-calorie malnutrition reduces hepatic synthesis of **albumin, prealbumin and transferrin**, and impairs immunity so **lymphocyte count falls**. Low oncotic pressure explains the edema, in the absence of kidney or liver disease.

idea.rule: Malnutrition: low visceral proteins (albumin, prealbumin, transferrin) and low lymphocytes with wasting; edema from low oncotic pressure.
also: Prealbumin has a short half-life and tracks recent intake
Kwashiorkor: edema and fatty liver with preserved fat stores
Marasmus: wasting without edema
Nephrotic syndrome and cirrhosis also lower albumin, with their own clues

stem: A 6-day-old breast-fed boy has vomiting after feeds, jaundice, an enlarged liver and poor weight gain since birth. Plasma glucose is 38 mg/dL. He has never been transfused. His urine is tested with a copper-reduction method and a glucose oxidase dipstick, and red-cell enzyme activity is measured.
oneliner: 6-day-old breast-fed boy + vomiting, jaundice, hepatomegaly + glucose 38 mg/dL → urine reducing substance, glucose oxidase, red-cell GALT?
ask: Which set of results is most likely?

options.A: Reducing substance +, glucose oxidase +, red-cell GALT normal
options.B: Reducing substance +, glucose oxidase −, red-cell GALT low
options.C: Reducing substance −, glucose oxidase −, red-cell GALT low
options.D: Reducing substance +, glucose oxidase −, red-cell GALT normal
options.E: Reducing substance −, glucose oxidase +, red-cell GALT low

whyNot.A: Both tests positive is **glucosuria**; his **plasma glucose of 38** is far too low to spill glucose
whyNot.C: No reducing sugar in the urine would not fit a baby who became **jaundiced with hepatomegaly** while taking **lactose** in breast milk
whyNot.D: Galactosuria with normal GALT is **galactokinase deficiency**, which causes only cataracts, not **jaundice, hepatomegaly and hypoglycemia**
whyNot.E: A positive glucose oxidase test means **glucosuria**, excluded by his **hypoglycemia**

answer: Reducing substance positive, glucose oxidase negative, red-cell GALT low (classic galactosemia)
why: In **classic galactosemia** (GALT deficiency) galactose from breast-milk lactose builds up with **galactose-1-phosphate**, injuring the liver and spilling into urine. Galactose is a **reducing sugar**, so the copper-reduction test is positive, but **glucose oxidase is specific for glucose**, so that test is negative; **red-cell GALT** activity confirms the enzyme defect.

idea.rule: Reducing substance positive with glucose oxidase negative means a non-glucose sugar in the urine.
also: Hereditary fructose intolerance: reducing substance positive after fructose intake, glucose oxidase negative
Essential fructosuria and pentosuria give the same pattern
Diabetes mellitus: both tests positive
Galactokinase deficiency also gives galactosuria with a negative glucose oxidase test, but only cataracts

stem: A 3-day-old boy, normal at birth, vomits and becomes lethargic with fast breathing a day after feeds were started. Blood gas shows respiratory alkalosis, BUN is low, and plasma ammonia is many times normal. His mother's brother died in the first week of life; his mother is well.
oneliner: 3M + day 3 vomiting, lethargy, fast breathing after feeds + resp alkalosis + low BUN + ↑↑ ammonia + maternal uncle died in infancy → which labs?
ask: Which set of laboratory results is most likely?

options.A: Ammonia ↑, citrulline ↓, urine orotic acid normal
options.B: Ammonia ↑, citrulline ↑, argininosuccinate ↑ in plasma and urine
options.D: Ammonia ↑, citrulline very markedly ↑, no argininosuccinate
options.E: Ammonia normal, urine orotic acid ↑, megaloblastic anemia

whyNot.A: Low citrulline with **normal orotic acid** is CPS I deficiency, which is autosomal recessive and does not explain the **maternal uncle** who died
whyNot.B: Argininosuccinate lyase deficiency is **autosomal recessive**; a sick boy whose **mother's brother** died points to an X-linked defect
whyNot.D: Very high citrulline is argininosuccinate synthetase deficiency, which is **autosomal recessive** and does not fit the **maternal uncle** pattern
whyNot.E: Ammonia would be normal, but this boy has **ammonia many times normal with respiratory alkalosis**

answer: Ammonia ↑, citrulline ↓, urine orotic acid ↑ (ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency)
why: The family history through the **mother's brother** marks an **X-linked** urea cycle defect, which is **OTC deficiency**. Carbamoyl phosphate cannot enter the cycle, so **ammonia rises** and **citrulline falls**, and the surplus carbamoyl phosphate leaves the mitochondrion and is made into **orotic acid**.

idea.rule: A urea cycle defect gives high ammonia with respiratory alkalosis; the citrulline level and urine orotic acid tell you where the block is.
also: CPS I deficiency: low citrulline, normal orotic acid
Argininosuccinate synthetase deficiency (citrullinemia): very high citrulline
Argininosuccinate lyase deficiency: argininosuccinate in plasma and urine
OTC is the only urea cycle defect that is X-linked

stem: A 35-year-old man has firm nodular swellings over both Achilles tendons and a pale ring around the edge of each cornea. His father had a myocardial infarction at 40. He is not diabetic and does not drink alcohol.
oneliner: 35M + Achilles tendon swellings + corneal arcus + father MI at 40 → which lipid panel?
ask: Which fasting lipid pattern is most likely?

options.C: Chylomicrons and triglycerides ↑, creamy layer on standing
options.D: Total cholesterol and triglycerides both ↑, with ↑ IDL remnants
options.E: LDL cholesterol and triglycerides both very ↓

whyNot.B: Raised **triglycerides with normal LDL** does not cause tendon xanthomas or arcus at 35
whyNot.C: A **creamy top layer** (chylomicrons) gives pancreatitis and eruptive xanthomas, not tendon xanthomas with early MI
whyNot.D: Remnant disease gives **palmar and tuberoeruptive xanthomas** with raised triglycerides; tendon xanthomas with isolated LDL excess fit better
whyNot.E: Very low lipids (abetalipoproteinemia) cause **fat malabsorption**, the opposite of xanthomas and a family history of early MI

answer: LDL cholesterol markedly raised with normal triglycerides (type IIa pattern, familial hypercholesterolemia)
why: **Tendon xanthomas**, **corneal arcus before 45**, and a father with a **premature MI** suggest **familial hypercholesterolemia**. Faulty LDL receptors leave LDL in the blood, so **LDL and total cholesterol are very high** while **triglycerides are normal**.

idea.rule: Tendon xanthomas plus early coronary disease means isolated LDL excess (type IIa).
also: LDL receptor mutation: autosomal dominant, heterozygotes have cholesterol around 300 to 400 mg/dL
Apo B-100 or PCSK9 gain-of-function gives the same picture
Homozygotes have cholesterol above 700 mg/dL and MI in childhood
Type IIb (combined) adds raised VLDL and triglycerides

stem: A 2-year-old boy has a vomiting illness and takes nothing by mouth for 18 hours, then becomes lethargic and has a seizure. Serum glucose is 28 mg/dL, ALT is mildly raised, plasma free carnitine is low, and the liver edge is felt 3 cm below the costal margin. Lactate and uric acid are normal.
oneliner: 2M + 18 h fast + lethargy, seizure + glucose 28 + hepatomegaly + low carnitine + normal lactate and uric acid → which labs?
ask: Which set of laboratory results is expected during this episode?

options.A: Glucose ↓, ketones ↑, lactate and uric acid normal

whyNot.A: High ketones mean fat is being burned; **low free carnitine** with an enlarged liver and fasting hypoglycemia points to a block in fat oxidation
whyNot.B: **Lactate and uric acid are normal** here, which argues against the glycogen storage disease that raises both
whyNot.C: Low citrulline with **raised orotic acid** is a urea cycle (OTC) pattern and does not explain a **glucose of 28** after fasting
whyNot.D: He is **hypoglycemic** (glucose 28), not hyperglycemic, so this is not insulin deficiency

answer: Hypoketotic hypoglycemia with dicarboxylic aciduria (fatty acid oxidation defect, such as LCAD or MCAD deficiency)
why: With no oral intake the body should switch to **beta-oxidation and ketone production**. In a **fatty acid oxidation defect** the liver cannot do this, so glucose is used up and **ketones stay low** while unoxidized fatty acids are diverted to **dicarboxylic acids** in the urine.

idea.rule: Fasting hypoglycemia with low ketones means the liver cannot oxidize fat.
also: MCAD deficiency: raised octanoylcarnitine
Carnitine deficiency: weakness and cardiomyopathy as well
Long-chain defects (LCAD, LCHAD): cardiomyopathy and rhabdomyolysis
Treatment is to avoid fasting and give frequent carbohydrate feeds

stem: A 1-week-old girl feeds poorly, vomits and becomes lethargic. Blood pH is 7.15 with bicarbonate 8 mEq/L and a wide anion gap. Plasma ammonia is 10 times normal, she has ketones in the urine, glucose is low, and serum lactate is normal. A sister died at 10 days of age.
oneliner: 1F + poor feeding, vomiting, lethargy + pH 7.15, HCO3 8, wide gap + ammonia ×10 + ketosis + low glucose + normal lactate + sibling death → which disorder?
ask: Which type of disorder does this laboratory pattern indicate?

whyNot.A: Gives hyperammonemia with **respiratory alkalosis**, not a **pH of 7.15 with bicarbonate 8** and ketosis
whyNot.C: Gives a **normal anion gap** acidosis with **no hyperammonemia**; this girl has a wide gap and ammonia ×10
whyNot.D: A storage disease builds up slowly over months, not a **first-week ketoacidosis with ammonia ×10**
whyNot.E: Mitochondrial disease gives a **lactic** acidosis, and her **lactate is normal** despite pH 7.15

answer: Organic acidemia (such as propionic or methylmalonic acidemia)
why: A baby with **wide anion gap acidosis, ketosis, and hyperammonemia** has an **organic acidemia**. The blocked pathway lets an organic acid accumulate (anion gap and ketones) and its CoA ester inhibits the urea cycle, so **ammonia also rises**.

idea.rule: High ammonia plus severe metabolic acidosis suggests organic acidemia; high ammonia plus respiratory alkalosis suggests a urea cycle defect.
also: Propionic acidemia: propionyl-CoA carboxylase deficiency
Methylmalonic acidemia: methylmalonyl-CoA mutase deficiency
Both block the path that carries propionyl-CoA from odd-chain fatty acids, valine, isoleucine, methionine and threonine
Newborn screening with acylcarnitines picks them up

stem: A 5-day-old breast-fed boy feeds poorly and vomits, then becomes lethargic and arches his back. His urine has a sweet, burnt-sugar odor. He has ketoacidosis and no hyperammonemia.
oneliner: 5M + poor feeding, vomiting, opisthotonus + sweet burnt-sugar urine → which findings?
ask: Which plasma and urine findings are expected?

options.A: Phenylalanine ↑ in plasma, with phenylketones in the urine
options.B: Methionine and homocysteine ↑ in plasma, with homocystine in the urine
options.C: Normal plasma amino acids, with neutral amino acids ↑ in the urine
options.D: Branched-chain amino acids ↑ in plasma, their ketoacids in urine
options.E: Glycine ↑ in plasma and CSF, with normal urine ketoacids

whyNot.A: Phenylketonuria gives a **musty odor** and a gradual developmental picture rather than a sweet smell with neonatal ketoacidosis
whyNot.B: Homocystinuria causes **lens dislocation and thrombosis**, not a burnt-sugar odor in the first week
whyNot.C: Neutral aminoaciduria is a **benign transport defect** with rash and ataxia, not encephalopathy with ketoacidosis
whyNot.E: Nonketotic hyperglycinemia gives seizures without the **ketoacidosis and sweet odor** seen here

answer: Leucine, isoleucine and valine raised in plasma, with branched-chain ketoacids in urine (maple syrup urine disease)
why: A **sweet burnt-sugar odor** with neonatal **encephalopathy and ketoacidosis** is **maple syrup urine disease**. Deficient **branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase** lets **leucine, isoleucine and valine** and their ketoacids build up and spill into the urine.

idea.rule: Sweet-smelling urine in a sick newborn means the branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase is blocked.
also: Needs thiamine (B1) as a cofactor; some patients respond to it
Treat with a diet restricting leucine, isoleucine and valine
Leucine is the most neurotoxic
Branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase shares its cofactors (B1, B2, B3, B5, lipoic acid) with pyruvate dehydrogenase

stem: A 4-month-old girl is floppy and feeds slowly. She has a large tongue, an enlarged heart on chest x-ray, a short PR interval on ECG, and a raised creatine kinase. Her liver is not enlarged.
oneliner: 4F + floppy, macroglossia, cardiomegaly, short PR, ↑CK, no hepatomegaly → which lab result?
ask: Which laboratory result is expected on fasting?

options.A: Fasting glucose, lactate and uric acid all normal
options.B: Fasting hypoglycemia with lactic acidosis and high uric acid
options.C: Fasting hypoglycemia with ketosis and normal lactate
options.E: Fasting hypoglycemia with low ketones and dicarboxylic aciduria

whyNot.B: Von Gierke disease gives this pattern with a **big liver**, and her liver is not enlarged
whyNot.C: Cori disease (debranching enzyme) gives ketotic hypoglycemia with **hepatomegaly**, and her liver is normal size
whyNot.D: A urea cycle defect causes **vomiting and encephalopathy**, not cardiomegaly with a large tongue and short PR
whyNot.E: Fat oxidation defects cause **fasting crises with an enlarged liver**; macroglossia and a short PR point to stored glycogen instead

answer: Normal fasting glucose, lactate and uric acid (Pompe disease)
why: **Floppy infant, macroglossia, cardiomegaly, short PR** is **Pompe disease** (acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency). Only **lysosomal** glycogen breakdown is lost, so **cytosolic glycogenolysis works** and fasting glucose, lactate and uric acid stay normal.

idea.rule: Pompe disease is a lysosomal glycogen disease with normal blood glucose, unlike the liver glycogen diseases.
also: Von Gierke (G6Pase): hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis, high uric acid
Cori disease (debranching enzyme): milder hypoglycemia, normal lactate
McArdle (muscle phosphorylase): no lactate rise with ischemic exercise
Enzyme replacement therapy with alglucosidase alfa helps Pompe disease

stem: A newborn boy is very floppy from birth, has seizures, a high forehead with a flat face, an enlarged liver, and direct hyperbilirubinemia with raised transaminases. Ultrasound shows small renal cysts.
oneliner: Newborn M + severe hypotonia, seizures, high forehead, flat face, hepatomegaly, direct hyperbilirubinemia, renal cysts → which biochemical finding?

options.A: Glucocerebroside ↑ in macrophages, with high chitotriosidase
options.B: Sphingomyelin ↑ in tissues, with cherry-red macula
options.C: Very-long-chain fatty acids and phytanic acid ↑
options.D: Dermatan and heparan sulfate ↑ in urine

whyNot.A: Gaucher disease causes **hepatosplenomegaly and bone crises**, not a floppy newborn with a flat face and renal cysts
whyNot.B: Niemann-Pick has a **cherry-red macula** and neuro regression, without a flat face and renal cysts
whyNot.D: Dermatan and heparan sulfate buildup gives **coarse features** that develop over months, not a dysmorphic face present **from birth**
whyNot.E: Mitochondrial disease raises **lactate** but does not cause the **dysmorphic face with renal cysts** and liver disease

answer: Very-long-chain fatty acids, phytanic acid and pipecolic acid raised (Zellweger syndrome)
why: A hypotonic newborn with **dysmorphic face, liver disease and renal cysts** has **Zellweger syndrome** (peroxisome biogenesis defect). With peroxisomes missing, **very-long-chain fatty acids** and **phytanic acid** accumulate and **plasmalogens fall**.

idea.rule: Peroxisome failure means very-long-chain fatty acids and phytanic acid pile up.
also: Adrenoleukodystrophy: X-linked, VLCFA accumulation, adrenal insufficiency
Refsum disease: phytanic acid alone, retinitis pigmentosa, ataxia
Plasmalogen synthesis needs peroxisomes
Zellweger is autosomal recessive

stem: A 3-year-old boy has delayed motor milestones, writhing movements of the limbs, and has started to bite his lips and fingers. His mother also reports occasional blood in his urine.
oneliner: 3M + motor delay, writhing movements, biting lips and fingers, hematuria → which finding?
ask: Which blood and urine finding is expected?

options.A: Serum uric acid ↓, with xanthine in the urine
options.B: Urine orotic acid ↑, with megaloblastic anemia
options.C: Hexagonal cystine crystals in the urine
options.D: Urine that darkens on standing from homogentisic acid
options.E: Serum uric acid ↑, with urate crystals in the urine

whyNot.A: Low urate from **xanthine oxidase deficiency** gives xanthine stones, not self-biting with dystonia
whyNot.B: Orotic aciduria causes **megaloblastic anemia** that does not respond to B12, not self-mutilation
whyNot.C: **Cystine stones** cause hematuria but do not explain the neurologic picture
whyNot.D: Alkaptonuria produces **dark urine and arthritis** in adults, not self-injury in an infant

answer: Raised serum uric acid with urate crystals in the urine (HGPRT deficiency, Lesch-Nyhan syndrome)
why: **Dystonia, developmental delay and self-biting** in a boy is **Lesch-Nyhan syndrome**. **HGPRT deficiency** blocks purine salvage, so PRPP builds up and purine synthesis rises, causing **high uric acid** with urate stones and hematuria.

idea.rule: No HGPRT means no purine salvage, so purines go to uric acid.
also: X-linked recessive, so almost always boys
Gout and tophi develop from the high urate
Treat with allopurinol, which does not fix the neurologic features
Orange crystals in the diaper are a clue

stem: An 8-year-old boy has episodes of unsteady gait that come and go. After a summer outdoors he develops a scaly red rash on his face, neck and forearms. He has had no diarrhea, and he improves when given niacin.
oneliner: 8M + intermittent ataxia + rash on sun-exposed skin + responds to niacin → which urine finding?

options.A: Cystine, ornithine, lysine and arginine ↑ in urine
options.B: Neutral amino acids and tryptophan ↑ in urine
options.E: Glucose, phosphate and amino acids all ↑ in urine

whyNot.A: Cystinuria causes **kidney stones** and affects dibasic amino acids, with no rash or ataxia
whyNot.C: Phenylketonuria gives **intellectual disability and a musty odor**, without a photosensitive rash
whyNot.D: Alkaptonuria gives **dark urine and joint disease** later in life
whyNot.E: Fanconi syndrome adds **glucose and phosphate** loss and does not explain a sun rash that **improves with niacin**

answer: Neutral amino acids raised in urine (Hartnup disease)
why: A **pellagra-like photosensitive rash** with **intermittent ataxia** that responds to niacin is **Hartnup disease**. A defect of the **neutral amino acid transporter** in the gut and kidney causes **urinary loss of neutral amino acids**, including **tryptophan**, which is the precursor of niacin.

idea.rule: Poor tryptophan absorption means too little niacin, which causes a pellagra-like picture.
also: Carcinoid syndrome diverts tryptophan to serotonin and can cause pellagra
Isoniazid lowers B6 needed for niacin synthesis
Pellagra: dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia
Autosomal recessive

stem: A 2-year-old boy looked normal at birth, but over the first year his face has become coarse. He now has a large liver and spleen, an umbilical hernia, corneal haziness on examination, and is losing skills he had learned.
oneliner: 2M + normal at birth, coarsening face over first year + hepatosplenomegaly, umbilical hernia, corneal clouding + regression → which finding?

options.A: Keratan sulfate alone in the urine
options.B: Normal urine GAGs, high plasma lysosomal enzymes
options.D: Dermatan sulfate and heparan sulfate in urine

whyNot.A: Keratan sulfate alone is **Morquio syndrome**, which has severe skeletal changes but normal intelligence
whyNot.B: I-cell disease is **severe from birth** with gingival overgrowth; the course here is normal early, coarsening later
whyNot.C: Niemann-Pick has **hepatosplenomegaly and regression** but not a coarse face or corneal clouding
whyNot.E: Tay-Sachs causes regression with a cherry-red macula but **no organomegaly or coarse face**

answer: Dermatan sulfate and heparan sulfate in urine (Hurler syndrome, mucopolysaccharidosis I)
why: **Coarse facies, hepatosplenomegaly, corneal clouding and regression** after a normal start suggest **Hurler syndrome**. Deficient **alpha-L-iduronidase** blocks breakdown of **dermatan sulfate and heparan sulfate**, which spill into the urine.

idea.rule: A lysosomal glycosaminoglycan disease shows as coarse features plus urinary dermatan and/or heparan sulfate.
also: Hunter syndrome (iduronate sulfatase): X-linked, no corneal clouding, aggressive behavior
Hurler: alpha-L-iduronidase deficiency, corneal clouding
Morquio: keratan sulfate, normal intelligence
Treatment includes enzyme replacement and bone marrow transplant

stem: A tall 16-year-old girl has long thin fingers and complains of blurry vision. Her arm span exceeds her height, she has a mid-systolic click at the apex, her intelligence is normal, and she has no history of blood clots.
oneliner: 16F + tall, long fingers, blurry vision + arm span > height + apical click + normal IQ + no clots → which eye finding?

whyNot.A: Downward displacement is the pattern of **homocystinuria**, which has intellectual disability and clots
whyNot.B: An oil-drop cataract from birth suggests **galactosemia**, not a tall girl with a click
whyNot.D: A cherry-red spot occurs in **lysosomal storage disease** with neurologic regression
whyNot.E: **Optic atrophy** is a nerve problem and does not explain long fingers, arm span above height and a click

answer: Lens displaced upward and outward (superotemporal), as in Marfan syndrome
why: A tall girl with **long fingers, arm span above height and a mitral click** with **normal intelligence and no thrombosis** has **Marfan syndrome**. Fibrillin-1 is defective, so zonular fibers weaken and the lens drifts **up and out**.

idea.rule: Marfan lenses go up ("superotemporal"); homocystinuria lenses go down.
also: Marfan: aortic root dilation and dissection
Homocystinuria: downward lens, thrombosis, intellectual disability
Both are tall with long fingers
Marfan is autosomal dominant with FBN1 mutation

stem: A 5-year-old Nigerian boy has red-bronze skin and red hair, and his mother has noticed rapid horizontal eye movements since birth. He squints in bright light and has poor vision.
oneliner: 5M + Nigerian, red-bronze skin and red hair + nystagmus since birth + photophobia + poor vision → which eye finding?

whyNot.B: Lisch nodules are **iris hamartomas** of neurofibromatosis type 1, which does not lighten skin and hair
whyNot.C: A cherry-red macula is seen in **lysosomal storage disease** and retinal artery occlusion
whyNot.D: Lens dislocation fits a **tall connective tissue disorder**, not red-bronze skin and red hair
whyNot.E: Kayser-Fleischer rings reflect **copper deposition** in Wilson disease

why: **Hypopigmented skin and hair with nystagmus and photophobia** is **oculocutaneous albinism**. Without ocular melanin the **fovea fails to develop** normally, giving **poor acuity and congenital nystagmus**.

idea.rule: Melanin is needed for normal retinal development, so albinism comes with poor sight.
also: Reduced iris pigment gives photophobia and transillumination
Abnormal optic nerve crossing at the chiasm
Albinism raises risk of skin cancer
Red-bronze (rufous) albinism in Africans is OCA3 from TYRP1 mutation; classic OCA1 lacks tyrosinase

stem: A 38-year-old woman at 16 weeks' gestation has second-trimester serum screening. The fetus is later found to have trisomy 21.
oneliner: 38F + 16 weeks + second-trimester quad screen + fetus later has trisomy 21 → which quad screen pattern?
ask: Which quad screen pattern is expected?

whyNot.A: That is the **neural tube defect** pattern (high AFP alone); trisomy 21 lowers AFP
whyNot.B: That is the **trisomy 18** pattern; AFP, estriol and **hCG are all low**
whyNot.C: Mixed pattern that matches no common aneuploidy; trisomy 21 gives **low AFP**, not high
whyNot.D: Isolated low estriol suggests **placental sulfatase deficiency or Smith-Lemli-Opitz**; trisomy 21 also shifts AFP, hCG and inhibin A

answer: Low AFP, low estriol, high hCG, high inhibin A
why: In **Down syndrome** the quad screen shows **low AFP and low estriol** with **high hCG and high inhibin A**. Contrast trisomy 18, where **AFP, estriol and hCG all fall** and inhibin A is normal.

idea.rule: Down syndrome: two markers low, two high (hCG and inhibin A up).
also: Trisomy 18: AFP, estriol and hCG all low
Neural tube defect: AFP high
Abdominal wall defect: AFP high
Wrong gestational dates also alter the screen
